clinicalPearls: Often discovered incidentally in adolescence or adulthood on radiographs or after a fracture.
Type II (Albers-Schönberg disease) arises from heterozygous CLCN7 mutations, typically dominant-negative.
Classic radiographic signs are the rugger-jersey spine, bone-within-bone appearance and a dense skull base.
Fracture risk is increased despite dense bone because the bone is brittle, and healing may be slow.
Mandibular osteomyelitis, often after dental extraction, is a recognised complication.
Cranial nerve compression (optic, facial, auditory) can occur but is far less common than in the infantile form.
Marrow function is usually preserved, so significant anaemia is unusual.
Type I disease (activating LRP5 mutations) has high bone mass but no excess fractures, a key distinction from type II.
reference.pathophysiology: Autosomal dominant osteopetrosis type II (Albers-Schönberg disease) is caused by heterozygous, typically dominant-negative, mutations in CLCN7, which encodes a chloride-proton antiporter needed to acidify the osteoclast resorption lacuna. Because one allele retains function, osteoclast-mediated resorption is only partially impaired, giving a much milder phenotype than autosomal recessive disease: bone is abnormally dense yet poorly remodelled and mechanically brittle, while marrow function is usually preserved. Sclerosis is characteristically focal, producing endplate sclerosis of the vertebrae (rugger-jersey spine), bone-within-bone (endobone) appearances and a dense skull base. Penetrance and severity are variable, so relatives carrying the same mutation may range from asymptomatic to markedly fracture-prone. Autosomal dominant osteopetrosis type I, once grouped here, is now recognised as a distinct high-bone-mass disorder due to activating LRP5 mutations, characterised by a thickened skull vault and, importantly, no increase in fracture risk.
additionalDifferentials: Autosomal dominant osteopetrosis type I (LRP5-related high bone mass)
Osteoblastic metastases (for example prostate or breast) and myelofibrosis with osteosclerosis
additionalInvestigations: Targeted radiographs or skeletal survey for the characteristic sclerotic patterns
CLCN7 molecular testing, with LRP5 testing if type I is suspected
Serum calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase (usually normal)
Serum acid phosphatase and the brain isoenzyme of creatine kinase (often raised)
Audiometry and ophthalmological review where symptomatic
Panoramic dental imaging to assess mandibular osteomyelitis risk
redFlags: Pathological fracture with delayed or non-union
Mandibular pain, swelling or discharge suggesting osteomyelitis, especially after dental work
New cranial nerve deficit such as visual loss, facial weakness or hearing loss
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is essentially normal. Morbidity arises from fractures with impaired healing, mandibular osteomyelitis and occasional cranial nerve compression rather than from marrow failure.
pitfalls: Confusing type I (LRP5, no fracture risk) with fracture-prone type II (CLCN7)
Mistaking diffuse osteosclerosis for metastatic disease or Paget disease
Undertaking dental extraction without anticipating the osteomyelitis risk
Assuming asymptomatic relatives are unaffected, given the variable penetrance
management: Manage fractures with orthopaedic care, anticipating delayed union and difficult fixation because the dense bone is brittle
Avoid unnecessary dental extractions and maintain meticulous oral hygiene to reduce the risk of mandibular osteomyelitis
Treat mandibular osteomyelitis with prolonged antibiotics and conservative surgical debridement in conjunction with maxillofacial surgery
Monitor for cranial nerve compression with periodic audiometry and ophthalmological review, referring for surgical decompression if optic or auditory function is threatened
Provide analgesia and physiotherapy for bone pain and to maintain mobility and function
Offer genetic counselling and family assessment given autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance
Refer to clinical genetics and a metabolic bone specialist for confirmatory CLCN7 testing and long-term surveillance
